Notes

Skin & Soft-Tissue Lesions: The Big Picture

Skin is built from epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous fat, arteries, veins, hair follicles and nerves, and a tumor can arise from any of these components. Skin tumors divide broadly into benign vs malignant.

Benign · 4 common Hematoma (blood) Lipoma (fat) Sebaceous cyst (sebum) Abscess (pus)·Malignant · 3 major Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) Malignant melanoma·Skin & soft-tissue lesions can arise from any skin component·Vascular · 2 groups Hemangioma Vascular malformation Both benign; told apart by natural history
Key definition
Tumor = a mass / neoplasm. It does not necessarily mean cancer.
  • Picture of an elderly face with a crusted, ulcerated nodule on the cheek → keyed squamous cell carcinoma. 435

Types of Tumors

  • Benign
  • Malignant

Benign Tumors

  • Hematoma
  • Abbcess
  • Lipoma
  • Sebaceous cyst
Notes

Common Benign Lesions

Four lumps that come up again and again. Learn the row that separates each one from its look-alikes.

HematomaLipomaSebaceous cystAbscess
What it isBlood collection beneath skinBenign tumor of fatBlocked gland opening → sebum accumulatesLocalized infection / pus collection
CourseAfter trauma (minor trauma if anticoagulated)Chronic, slow-growingChronic / dormant; may become inflamedAcute
SymptomsBruising, or swelling that may expand; ± compressionPainless (spontaneous pain = worry)Painless unless inflamed / infectedVery painful, tender, erythema ± fever
Exam clueDiscoloration / expanding swellingMobile, soft-firm, compressiblePunctum; firmer; thick chalky sebumErythema ± ulceration / discharge
ImagingUS or MRI (X-ray poor)US or MRIClinical ± USUS ± MRI
ManagementObserve if stable; drain if expanding / compressingObserve; excise if concerning or cosmeticInflamed: antibiotics → excise later; else exciseI&D + antibiotics; pack, leave open

Hematoma

  • A hematoma is the result of a traumatic injury to skin or the tissues underneath the skin
  • When blood vessels under the skin are damaged and leak, the blood pools and results in a bruise
  • A hematoma forms as blood clots, resulting in swelling and pain
  • Usually no treatment required in most of the cases
  • Cold sponging and analgesics relieves pain and swelling
  • Swelling, skin discoloration and clots oozing from the wound after restarting anticoagulation → hematoma (printed "hamartoma" in the source). 441
Notes

Hematoma

Blood collection beneath the skin, usually after trauma. How much trauma it takes depends on the patient:

Normal patient
Usually needs significant trauma.
Anticoagulated patient
Minor trauma may cause a significant hematoma.

Presentation

Bruising / discoloration only, or
Swelling that may enlarge / expand.
Superficial collection → obvious mass; may also extend deeper.
Flat / stable hematoma usually causes no underlying compression.
An expanding one can compress what lies beneath (below).

Compression effects

Structure compressedEffect
Artery↓ Circulation → pallor, ↓ O2 saturation distally
NerveNumbness ± difficulty moving the affected part
Imaging rule of thumb
Hematoma is investigated mainly with US or MRI; X-ray does not show it well. In general: MRI is better for soft tissue, CT is better for bone.

Management

Observe
Stable, non-expanding, non-compressive hematoma.
Warm compress
Elevation if a limb is involved
Drain / evacuate
How: small skin incision + evacuation.
Expanding
Compressing artery, nerve or other structures
Enlargement threatens overlying skin

Lipoma

Notes

Lipoma

Most common benign soft-tissue tumor.
Benign tumor of fat; can occur anywhere (e.g. back, head).
Cause of localized formation usually unclear.
Chronic, slow-growing, painless swelling.
Size may change with body weight.
Pain uncommon: pressure on adjacent bone / nerve, or direct pressure / trauma.
Red flag
Spontaneous pain (without pressure or touch) is more concerning for malignancy than a typical lipoma.

Examination & investigation

Overlying skin usually normal.
Mobile from side to side.
Soft but somewhat firm (surrounding capsule); more compressible than a sebaceous cyst.
US or MRI if needed (MRI over CT for soft tissue).
Management & counselling
Most → observation.
Biopsy / excision if the diagnosis is concerning or the patient wants it removed; excision is commonly cosmetic.
Counsel: removal replaces the lump with a scar; surgery always leaves some scar.
  • History → Chronic swelling, painless rarely painful
  • Exam → located anywhere, No skin change , Mobile firm lesion
  • Investigation → US or CT scan if needed
  • Management → Rarely we do biopsy for it , Usually inside a capsule, 99.9 is benign they remove it for cosmetic

Sebaceous Cyst ine

Notes

Sebaceous Cyst

Mechanism
Obstruction of the sebaceous gland opening → sebaceous material accumulates. Usually chronic / dormant, but may become inflamed / infected. Common on the head / neck and hair-bearing areas.
High-yield picture / MCQ finding
Punctum = the characteristic small opening / dot over the lesion. See a punctum, think sebaceous cyst.

Look-alikes: it depends on whether it is inflamed

Cyst stateResemblesSymptoms
Non-inflamedLipomaUsually painless
Inflamed / infectedAbscessPainful

Sebaceous cyst vs lipoma on examination

FeatureLipomaSebaceous cyst
SurfaceNormal overlying skinPunctum
ConsistencySoft-firm (capsule); more compressibleFirmer, resists compression (depends on amount of contents)
ContentsFatThick, chalk-like sebum (not simple liquid)
Typical siteAnywhere (e.g. back, head)Head / neck, hair-bearing areas
Investigation Management Inflamed / infected Non-infectedUS or MRI → → Antibiotics first Inflammation settles Surgical excisionOften clinical ± US Surgical excision later
Don't excise during acute inflammationThe cyst wall becomes fragile → difficult to remove completely.
  • Hidradenitis suppurativa is a disease of the apocrine sweat glands (axilla, groin). 427 ×2

Sebaceous Cyst

  • History → Chronic swelling (acute ? Infected), painless (painful ? Infected)
  • Exam → Usually in the head, has a “punctum”, painful and inflamed and with discharge if infected
  • Investigation → US (But usually clinical)
  • Management → If infected then treat with Abx, then surgical lexcision. If not infected it can be excised

Abscess

Notes

Abscess

Localized infection / pus collection; can occur anywhere.

Acute, very painful swelling
Tenderness + erythema
May have ulceration / discharge
± Fever
± Leukocytosis
Investigation: US ± MRI when needed

Treatment

Incision & drainage

Antibiotics

Pack the wound, leave it open

Never close an abscess primarily after drainage
Residual bacteria / pus may remain despite cleaning. Leaving the wound open allows continued drainage.
  • History → acute swelling, painful, erythema +/- fever (sepsis)
  • Exam → tender, erythema and discharge
  • Investigation → US (But usually clinical)
  • Management → Incision and drainage and Abx (keep open and pack)

Skin Cancer

Notes

Malignant Skin Tumors

Three major types, which differ most in how aggressively they behave.

Basal cell carcinoma Least aggressive. Slow-growing; very low metastatic potential (essentially does not metastasize).·Squamous cell carcinoma More aggressive and faster- growing than BCC; more destructive appearance.·Malignant melanoma Most aggressive of the skin cancers discussed.

Less aggressive

More aggressive

  • Rodent ulcer = basal cell carcinoma. 426
Notes

BCC & SCC: Shared Risk Factors

Each risk factor maps onto a question to ask in the history.

Risk factorAsk about
Sun exposure (major risk factor)Occupation / nature of work
Childhood history of sunburnRecurrent sunburn
Light skin → greater skin-cancer riskSkin color
Immunosuppression / immunosuppressive drugsMedications, immunosuppression
  • Chemotherapy after an oncologic resection — the gift key is 3 weeks (slides: 10–14 days; doctor: ~2 weeks). Answer 3 weeks in this question. 438 ×6
  • Diagnosis
    • Biopsy types:
      • Punch
      • Incisional
      • Excisional
  • Treatment:
    • Moh’s micrographic surgery
    • Surgical excision: margins.
    • Destructive treatment ( cryosurgery-curettage and electrodessication- photodynamic treatment)
    • Radiotherapy (SCC)
Notes

BCC vs SCC

FeatureBasal cell carcinomaSquamous cell carcinoma
Most common inOtherwise normal patientsImmunocompromised / transplant patients
Typical sitesNose, eyelidsEar, around the lips
GrowthSlow; often present for years before significant growthFaster, more aggressive
AppearanceRelatively innocuous; recurrent small scab / flap; may show small ulcerationMore destructive; looks abnormal earlier in its course
MetastasisVery low potentialMore aggressive than BCC
Excision margin*0.5–1 cm1–2 cm
Extra optionsCryotherapy if surgery not toleratedRadiotherapy as additional treatment
Rule of thumb most common.Normal patient → BCC is the most common skin cancer. Immunocompromised or transplant patient → SCC is the
Rule of thumb: normal patient → BCC is the most common skin cancer. Immunocompromised/transplant patient → SCC is the most common.
Notes

Diagnosis: Biopsy

Skin cancer is confirmed by biopsy. Know what each type samples and its main limitation.

TypeWhat it doesUsed forKey pro / con
PunchPen-like punch removes a small cylinder of skin, about 2–3 mmSimple, minor procedureCon: samples a small % → may not represent the whole lesion
IncisionalRemoves part of the lesion; must be full thickness from surface downwardLarge lesionsCon: partial sample may not represent the entire tumor
ExcisionalRemoves the entire lesion, with a small margin (~2 mm in lecture)Small lesions, e.g. suspected small BCCPro: diagnosis + possible definitive removal in one step → may avoid a second surgery
FNAFine-needle aspirationDeeper structuresNot usual for superficial skin lesions
Notes

Treatment: Excision with Margins

The main treatment for BCC and SCC (and melanoma) is surgical excision with margins. The more aggressive the tumor, the wider the margin.

BCC SCC Melanoma 0 1 minimum margin upper end of range Worked example A 1-cm lesion with a 1-cm margin on each side needs an excision about 3 cm wide in total. The margin is added on both sides.231 cm margin ≈ 3 cm total width4 cm 1 cm lesion0.5–1 cm 1–2 cm 2–4 cm 1 cm margin

*Margins are the lecture-stated figures. Published guidelines vary with tumor type and risk, so check which values your exam expects.

Notes

Mohs Micrographic Surgery

A tissue-sparing technique for sites where standard wide margins would remove important tissue and cause major functional or cosmetic loss, e.g. the eyelid or nose.

1 Remove the tumor

2 Map the margins

3 Examine margins

histologically

4 Positive margin? Take more tissue only from that area, then repeat

AdvantagesDrawbacks
Very accurate: more complete margin examination than routine sampling / frozen sectionTime-consuming: ~1–1.5 h per stage; whole procedure ~4–5 h
Minimizes removal of normal tissueNeeds a specialized center with close surgeon / dermatologist–histopathologist coordination
Ideal for eyelid, nose and similar sites Non-surgical & additional treatmentNot available everywhere
Cryotherapy / destructive treatment Consider when the patient cannot tolerate surgery.Radiotherapy Additional treatment, particularly for SCC.
  • Melanoma
Notes

Malignant Melanoma

Evaluated as a pigmented / melanocytic lesion; the key differential is a benign nevus vs melanoma. It is the most aggressive of the skin cancers discussed.

  • Most common type of melanoma → superficial spreading melanoma. 429 ×4
Notes

ABCDE Features

FeatureFavors benignConcerning for melanoma
AAsymmetrySymmetricAsymmetric
BBorderSmooth, regularIrregular / ill-defined
CColorUniformMultiple shades / color variation
DDiameterSmaller> ¼ inch (~6 mm); larger = more concerning
EEvolutionStable over yearsChange in size or appearance
Don't be reassured by size alone
A stable dark lesion is less concerning than an evolving one, but even a small suspicious pigmented lesion should be assessed, because melanoma is highly aggressive.
  • Elderly man, scaly erythematous lesion with irregular borders on the sun-exposed dorsum of the forearm → actinic keratosis (pre-malignant → SCC). 436 Final
Notes

Prognosis Depends on Depth

Prognosis and staging are strongly related to tumor depth: the deeper the tumor, the markedly worse the outlook.

~100% 5-year survival

< 1 mm

~50% 5-year survival

> 4 mm

Treatment
Surgical excision with margins, the widest of the three skin cancers: 2–4 cm in the lecture's comparison (vs 0.5–1 cm BCC, 1–2 cm SCC).

Vascular Lesions

  • Hemangioma
  • Vascular malformations:
    • High flow
    • Low flow
      • Venous malformations
      • Capillary malformations
      • Lymphatic malformations
Notes

Vascular Skin Lesions

Two major groups. The presentation and natural history are what tell them apart.

At birthEarly lifeFollowing years
HemangiomaAbsent or only minimally apparentRapid proliferation in the first year, disproportionate to the child's growth; then stopsGradual involution
Vascular malformationPresentGrows proportionally with the child; no rapid proliferative phasePersists; no spontaneous involution
Key distinction
Hemangioma: absent at birth → rapid growth → involutes.
Malformation: present at birth → grows with child → persists.
Management
Both are generally benign vascular lesions; treatment is often driven mainly by cosmetic considerations.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

The highest-yield distinctions. If you can explain each line without looking, you know this lecture.

1 Tumor ≠ cancer: a tumor is any mass / neoplasm, and skin tumors can arise from any skin component.
2 Hematoma: anticoagulated patients bleed after minor trauma. Observe if stable; drain if expanding, compressing
artery / nerve, or threatening the skin.
3 Imaging: US or MRI for soft-tissue lumps; X-ray misses hematoma. MRI = soft tissue, CT = bone.
4 Lipoma: most common benign soft-tissue tumor; mobile, compressible, painless. Spontaneous pain → think
malignancy.
5 Sebaceous cyst = punctum. Firmer than a lipoma; mimics lipoma when quiet, abscess when inflamed. Inflamed →
antibiotics first, excise later (fragile wall).
6 Abscess: I&D + antibiotics; pack and leave open, never close primarily.
7 BCC: most common in normal patients; nose / eyelids; slow; essentially no metastasis.
8 SCC: most common in immunosuppressed / transplant patients; ear / lips; more aggressive; radiotherapy as
adjunct.
9 Margins (lecture): BCC 0.5–1, SCC 1–2, melanoma 2–4 cm, added to both sides of the lesion.
10 Biopsy: punch (2–3 mm, may miss), incisional (large lesions, full thickness), excisional (small lesions, diagnose +
treat).
11 Mohs: tissue-sparing, very accurate, for eyelid / nose; slow (~4–5 h) and needs a specialized center.
12 Melanoma ABCDE (D > 6 mm); prognosis = depth: < 1 mm ~100%, > 4 mm ~50% 5-year survival.
13 Hemangioma appears after birth, grows fast, involutes; vascular malformation is present at birth, grows with the
child, persists.

Part B — Wound healing

Objectives

  • Types of wounds
  • Wound healing and its types
  • Phases of wound healing
  • Factors affecting wound healing
  • Abnormal scarring
    • Keloids
    • Hypertrophic scars
  • Multivitamins in a well-nourished patient → no effect on healing. 437 Final ×2
  • Keloid after sternotomy → expect itching (keyed A; one version also marked D, size fluctuation). 439 Final
Notes

How to Use This Guide

Teal box Lecture fact or mechanism·Gold box Rule of thumb, timing or treatment·Red box Warning, exception or high-risk point·EXAM Exam or OSCE tip, kept apart from lecture content
  • The main difference: keloids extend beyond the original zone of injury. 429 ×3

Definitions

  • Wound: disruption of normal anatomical structure and function
  • Acute wound: proceeds through an orderly and timely reparative process to restore function and anatomical integrity (3-4 wk)
  • Chronic wound: proceeds through a reparative process without establishing a sustained anatomic and functional result (beyond 6 wk)
Speaker notes

Hiii

  • Healing: Response of an organism to a physical disruption in an organ or a tissue to repair the defect

Abnormal Healing

  • Overgrowth → keloid or hypertrophic scar
  • Undergrowth → wide or thin or chronic unstable
  • Abnormal pigmentation → hypo/hyper
Speaker notes

Hiii

  • Burn-scar contracture release at the elbow: the reconstruction most likely to re-contract → split-thickness skin graft (thin grafts contract most; flaps contract least). 435 ×3

Scar formation

  • Substitution of a different cellular matrix as a patch to immediately re-establish both a physical and a physiological continuity of the injured organ

Regeneration

  • Recreating the original organ by the developmental process which created it

Scar formation vs. Regeneration ??

Phases of Normal Wound Healing

1. Hemostasis

2. Inflammatory phase

3. Proliferative phase

4. Remodeling phase

  • Wound contracture is a process that occurs throughout the healing process starting from the proliferative phase
  • The longest phase of wound healing → remodelling. 438 Final
  • Infected, opened and dressed wound → prolonged proliferative phase 432 Final ×3; huge infected necrotic sacral ulcer in a bed-bound diabetic → inflammatory and proliferative phases both increased. 429 Final

EXAM

Scar timing rule
The scar keeps changing for up to 1 year, so assess the final scar appearance at ~1 year.
Avoid definitive scar revision before ~1 year when possible.
During remodeling, creams, medications and lasers may improve appearance.

Epithelial Repair

  • Epithelial continuity is reestablished across a wound

Wound Contraction

  • Active, normal & essential part of healing
  • Rate depends on the number of myofibroblasts

    • Undesirable result of healing due to excessive contraction and fibrosis
Notes

Contraction vs Contracture

FeatureWound contractionContracture
What it isNormal reduction in wound sizePathological deformity caused by excessive contraction
MechanismMyofibroblasts, fibroblast-like cells with contractile (myosin) elements, pull the wound edges togetherThe same process, but excessive
EffectBeneficial: a large wound becomes progressively smallerFunctional limitation and deformity
Where it mattersAny open woundWounds crossing joints, mouth, nose, ear and other orifices, including the perianal region
High-risk sites
Wounds over joints or orifices need better wound coverage and management to minimize contracture.

Notes

Factors Affecting Wound Healing

There are two groups: local factors at the wound and systemic factors in the patient. Several act on a specific phase, which is summarised in the matrix at the end of this section.

Local Factors

FactorHow it impairs healingPhases hitPractical point
InfectionPersistent bacteria and inflammation; interferes with and degrades newly formed collagenInflammation + proliferation (phases 2 & 3)Infection in the first month → poorer scar
RadiationDamages the cells involved throughout healingAll phasesLeave a ~3-week gap before/after surgery (see below)
Blood supplyAll healing cells and nutrients depend on vascular delivery: peripheral vascular disease, poor local perfusionPotentially allSmoking acts through this route (↓ perfusion)
Nerve supply / repeated traumaSensory loss doesn't stop healing directly, but causes repetitive unnoticed trauma that re- injures tissue in the first weeksDelays progressionDiabetic neuropathy, polyneuropathy, severed peripheral nerve
Moisture / dressingA covered, moist wound is better than an exposed one: less contamination, no drying/cracking, healing cells work betterHealing environmentNot one dressing forever: change regularly, often every 2–3 days
TemperatureTemperature of the wound environment affects healingHealing environmentMaintain an appropriate wound/operative environment
Timing rule: cancer therapy and surgery (lecture figures)
~3 wk
Radiation. Before surgery: allow ~3 weeks for tissue recovery (when oncologically acceptable). After surgery: allow ~3 weeks for initial collagen deposition before starting radiation.
~2 wk
Chemotherapy. Separate chemotherapy and surgery by about 2 weeks before/after, when clinically possible.

Systemic Factors

Managing the high-risk patient
Systemic factors are either congenital/non-modifiable or acquired/modifiable. For non-modifiable or high-risk conditions:
Principle: the risk may not be eliminated, but it can be anticipated and minimized.
Counsel the patient about increased complication risk.
Avoid unnecessary elective surgery when risk outweighs benefit.
Take additional precautions.
Consider leaving sutures/support in place longer.

Local factors

  • Infection

Systemic factors : congenital

  • Pseudoxanthoma elasticum
  • Ehler-Danlos syndrome
    • AD, defect in synthesis, structure and cross linkage of collagen
  • Cutis laxa
  • Progeria
  • Werner syndrome
  • Epidermolysis bullosa

Systemic factors : Acquired

  • Nutrition
  • Pharmacological
  • Endocrine abnormalities
  • Age
  • Smoking

Nutrition

Vitamin A

  • Deficiency delays wound healing
    • 25,00 0 IU po OD increases tensile strength
    • 200,000 IU topical Q8 increases epitheliazation

Vitamin C

  • Collagen synthesis
  • Scurvy :
    • Immature fibroblasts
    • Deficient collagen synthesis
    • Capillary hemorrhage
    • Decreased tensile strength

Vitamin E

  • Antioxidant
  • Membrane stabilizer
  • Large doses may inhibit healing but unproven to reduce scarring

Zinc

  • Cofactor for many enzymes
  • Deficiency causes impaired epithelial and fibroblast proliferation

Pharmacological

  • Steroids decrease inflammation and subsequent wound healing
  • NSAIDS decrease collagen synthesis and inhibit platelet aggregation
  • Antineoplastic agents decrease fibroblasts proliferation and wound contraction
    • Few or no adverse reaction if administered 10-14 days after wound closure

Endocrine abnormalities

  • Diabetics often have delayed wound healing
  • Neuropathy rather than small vessel occlusive disease may be responsible for delayed healing

Age

  • Rate of cell multiplication decreases with age
  • All stages of healing are protracted in elderly
  • Healed wounds have less tensile strength in elderly

Smoking

  • Nicotine causes vasoconstriction decreasing perfusion
  • CO shifts oxygen dissociation curve and reduces tissue oxygenation

Infection

  • Wounds with over 10 ⁵ organisms per gram of tissue are considered infected and are unlikely to heal without further treatment

Radiation

  • Causes endothelial cell , capillary and arteriole damage
  • Irradiated fibroblasts secrete less collagen and extracellular matrix
  • Lymphatics are destroyed resulting in edema and risk of infection

Blood supply

  • Decreased tissue perfusion results in decreased wound oxygenation
  • Fibroblasts are oxygen-sensitive and their function is reduced in hypoxic states

Decreased oxygen delivery to tissue reduces :

  • Collagen formation
    • Extracellular matrix deposition
    • Angiogenesis
    • Epithliazation

Types of wound healing

  • Primary intention
    • Primary closure of the wound → least amount of scarring
  • Secondary intention
    • Heal by granulation, contraction and epithelialization
  • Tertiary intention (delayed primary closure)
    • Used for contaminated wounds

Types of Wound Healing

Primary intentionSecondary intentionTertiary (delayed primary closure)

OSCE
The border relationship is the classic differentiating point: keloid = beyond the wound border; hypertrophic = within it.
